changes.change: 505 products whose FDA filing names a contract manufacturer (Allure Labs, COSMAX, Prime Packaging, Fallien, Cross Brands and others) now show the brand and name printed on the package front, read from the filed artwork. Titanium dioxide or zinc oxide printed again as a colorant in the inactive list (CI 77891, 'may contain') is kept in the list. A misspelled single ingredient name ('Methyparaben', 'Proplyene Glycol') is shown spelled right.
changes.why: Accuracy: parents and experts look a product up by the brand on the package; the post-fix audit (2026-10-24) found these as its most common minor errors.

changes.change: A second blind audit of 300 different labels (after v3.8) found smaller gaps, now fixed: 'Diethylhexyl 2' + '6-Naphthalate' rejoined as one name (its UV booster warning was lost); coneflower counts as a ragweed-family plant; a kit whose products print different SPFs shows the lowest; a package that says soy-free drops the soy warning for lecithin of unstated source; 'sr-' recombinant proteins (vegan collagen) are not animal-derived; label footnotes stuck to a name ('*Denotes') are removed; when a printed name does not itself give a warning, the warning cites the FDA filing name it comes from; an SPF under 15 read from the package or the name gives the below-SPF-15 warning.
changes.why: Accuracy: each change came from the post-fix stratified audit (2026-10-24). Same rules for every product.

changes.change: A blind audit of 300 labels against their package artwork found rule gaps that each reached many labels, now fixed: BHT gave no warning (617 labels); avobenzone and ensulizole printed under their INCI names among the inactives gave no warning; Ext. Violet 2, trolamine, DEA-cetyl phosphate, emu oil, snail secretion, isopropyl alcohol, cyclomethicone 4, oligoglucosides, Optiphen and misspelled perfluoro- names now match; plain lecithin gives the soy warning with 'source not stated'; synthetic aroma chemicals give the fragrance warning even when an essential oil is also listed; diethylhexyl 2,6-naphthalate counts as a UV booster. A kit's list now keeps every product's ingredients. Where two reads of the package agree on the actives and the filing differs, the package's actives are shown. A strength misread (titanium dioxide 4% shown as 19.5% when the panel lists the names before the numbers) was fixed on 18 labels. 'Oil spray' on the package front marks a spray; a spray word only in label text on a package a person read as a lotion does not. 'No artificial fragrance' is no longer read as a named scent. A lactic/glycolic acid copolymer is not free glycolic acid.
changes.why: Accuracy: each change came from the final stratified audit (2026-10-24) or a sweep for the same gap across the database. Same rules for every product.

changes.change: Every warning's explanation and source were checked against the primary source (EU regulation text, CFR, FDA orders, ACDS, AAP/AAD, peer-reviewed papers): 46 explanations reworded to say no more than the source supports, all 64 citations made specific, and 20 rules now say plainly that they are our judgment. Matching fixed where four random label audits found gaps: plant-family and food-allergen names the old dictionary missed (marigold, burdock, soy lecithin, almond oil, beeswax, coconut-derived ingredients), Polycrylene as a UV absorber, sunscreen + insect repellent products, and three false matches (Ligularia fischeri as fish, Poria cocos as coconut, gardenia as jasmine). Broad Spectrum is no longer read from the Drug Facts direction sentence.
changes.why: Accuracy: each change came from a source check or an audit of labels against their package artwork. Same rules for every product.

changes.change: The check now reads the ingredient list printed on the label, not names that appear only in the FDA filing. A filing name still counts when it is a printed ingredient under another name or says what it comes from (soy or egg lecithin, fish collagen). Strengths come from the printed Drug Facts; a strength the filing gives per volume is not converted. One filing that covers several products says so. Also: methyldibromo glutaronitrile (banned in EU cosmetics) is flagged; an SPF under 15 gets the not-broad-spectrum flag; propylene glycol esters are not propylene glycol; seed oils are not essential oils; pain-relief creams are no longer listed as sunscreens.
changes.why: A check of 736 labels against their printed cartons found warnings resting on names only the FDA filing had (often another scent or an older formula), strengths converted from the filing's units (13.2% shown for a printed 12%), and kits whose products were merged. Each fix is the same rule for every brand.

changes.change: Three label checks added to 'Act on it': a sunscreen combined with an insect repellent (AAP), ingredients the EU restricts for children under 3 (salicylic acid, boric acid and borates), and fully fluorinated PFAS ingredients (state cosmetic bans since 2025). Each label's full text is now read for its Broad Spectrum claim and for the FDA Skin Cancer/Skin Aging Alert, which marks a sunscreen that is not broad spectrum or is below SPF 15. The EU fragrance-allergen check now covers the full list as extended in 2023 (Regulation (EU) 2023/1545), such as camphor, menthol, vanillin and citrus peel oils; when a label has only these and no fragrance, the summary says 'Contains an EU-listed fragrance allergen'.
changes.why: A review of what a baby-sunscreen check should catch found these on real labels and not yet covered.

changes.change: Each group now has one written test. 'Check if your child reacts' is limited to three named lists (ACDS Allergen of the Year, EU labelled fragrance allergens, US major food allergens), so alkyl glucosides, sulfites and isobornyl acrylate are added; ragweed-family plants, bee-derived ingredients, oat and drying alcohol move to 'Also in it'. Propyl/butylparaben and phototoxic citrus move to 'Act on it' (EU restrictions). Synthetic beeswax no longer counts as bee-derived; an essential oil must be an oil. Ingredient jobs now come from the EU CosIng register, reviewed twice.
changes.why: So that what we show first follows a test anyone can check, the same for every brand.

changes.change: 'Contains synthetic polymer microparticles' is now 'Contains a synthetic polymer powder (for texture)'.
changes.why: 'Microparticles' is a term defined in the EU microplastics restriction (Regulation (EU) 2023/2055). Whether that restriction applies is a product-by-product legal judgement a label cannot settle, so the check now states the ingredient fact only. Same rule for every product; the same ingredients are matched as before.
